**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Former Major League Baseball Most Valuable Player Miguel Tejada pleaded guilty in federal court Wednesday to lying to congressional investigators about the use of performance-enhancing drugs in the sport, marking another somber chapter in baseball's ongoing struggle with its "Steroid Era."

Tejada, 34, admitted to a misdemeanor charge of making misrepresentations to committee staff during a 2005 interview. The charge carries a maximum penalty of one year in prison, though federal prosecutors indicated they would not seek jail time as part of a plea agreement. Sentencing is scheduled for later this spring.

Standing before U.S. Magistrate Judge Alan Kay, the Dominican-born shortstop spoke softly as he acknowledged his actions. 

"I made a mistake," Tejada said through an interpreter outside the courthouse. "I apologize to the fans, to the young kids, and to the American people."

### The Lies to Capitol Hill

The charges stem from a December 2005 interview conducted in a Baltimore hotel room by investigators from the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. At the time, Congress was mounting a high-profile inquiry into pervasive drug use in professional sports, sparked in part by former slugger Jose Canseco's tell-all book.

During that interview, Tejada told committee staffers that he had never used performance-enhancing drugs and was unaware of any other players doing so.

However, federal prosecutors revealed that Tejada had, in fact, purchased approximately $3,100 worth of Human Growth Hormone (HGH) and anabolic steroids from former Oakland Athletics teammate Adam Piatt in 2003. While prosecutors noted there was no definitive evidence Tejada actually used the substances—Tejada claimed he threw them away without taking them—his failure to disclose the purchase to federal authorities constituted a crime.

Tejada’s name later surfaced in the 2007 Mitchell Report, the landmark investigation into drug use in MLB led by former Sen. George Mitchell, which prompted the Justice Department to open its investigation into his statements to Congress.

### A Fall from Grace for an MVP

The guilty plea is a dramatic fall from grace for one of baseball's most respected and durable stars of the 2000s. 

Tejada rose from impoverished origins in the Dominican Republic to become a cornerstone of the Oakland A’s "Moneyball" era. In 2002, he was named the American League MVP after driving in 131 runs and leading the A's to a 103-win season. A six-time All-Star, Tejada was revered not only for his offensive power and smooth defense but also for his extraordinary durability, once playing in 1,152 consecutive games—the fifth-longest streak in MLB history.

After his stint in Oakland, Tejada signed a massive six-year, $72 million contract with the Baltimore Orioles in 2004, where he continued to be a fan favorite before being traded to the Houston Astros in late 2007. 

### A Dark Week for Baseball

Tejada's court appearance comes during a particularly turbulent week for Major League Baseball. Just days prior, New York Yankees superstar Alex Rodriguez sent shockwaves through the sport by publicly admitting that he used performance-enhancing drugs from 2001 to 2003 while playing for the Texas Rangers.

Rodriguez's admission came after reports leaked that he was among 104 players who tested positive for banned substances during a anonymous 2003 survey test conducted by MLB to gauge the extent of drug use. 

While Rodriguez faces intense public scrutiny and a damaged legacy, Tejada’s case underscores the legal peril players face when federal authorities get involved. Tejada becomes the latest high-profile athlete to face federal criminal charges stemming from steroid inquiries, joining the likes of Marion Jones and Roger Clemens, who remains under federal scrutiny.

Major League Baseball issued a brief statement following Wednesday's proceedings, reiterating its commitment to a clean game: "We support the efforts of law enforcement to ensure truthfulness in legal proceedings. MLB remains steadfast in eradicating performance-enhancing substances from our sport."

As Tejada awaits sentencing, his legal troubles serve as a stark reminder that the shadows of baseball's drug-tainted past continue to loom large over its present.

**SPECIAL REPORT: THE MIGUEL TEJADA PED INVESTIGATION AND CONVICTION**

**WASHINGTON** — Former Major League Baseball (MLB) Most Valuable Player Miguel Tejada’s legal and professional downfall remains one of the most prominent legal cases stemming from the era of performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) in American sports. 

Below is a summary of the investigations, federal charges, court proceedings, and ultimate sentencing surrounding the former All-Star shortstop.

---

### **1. Origins of the Scandal: The 2005 Congressional Testimony**
In August 2005, amid growing public and political concern regarding widespread steroid use in baseball, staff members of the U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform interviewed Tejada. The interview took place in Baltimore, where Tejada was playing for the Orioles. 

When questioned by congressional investigators, Tejada explicitly denied ever using performance-enhancing drugs, purchasing them, or discussing their use with other players.

### **2. The Mitchell Report Contradictions (2007)**
Tejada’s statements were publicly challenged in December 2007 following the release of the landmark **Mitchell Report**, an independent investigation into PED use in MLB led by former U.S. Senator George Mitchell.

The report produced evidence directly contradicting Tejada's 2005 statements. Former Oakland Athletics teammate Adam Piatt testified to investigators that he had sold human growth hormone (HGH) and anabolic steroids to Tejada in 2003. Piatt provided physical evidence, including copies of canceled checks signed by Tejada totaling $3,100 for the substances. 

While the report did not definitively prove Tejada had ingested the substances, it demonstrated that he had solicited and purchased them—directly refuting his sworn statements to federal investigators.

### **3. Federal Charges and Court Case (2008–2009)**
Following the revelations in the Mitchell Report, the House Committee referred Tejada’s case to the U.S. Department of Justice to investigate whether he had committed perjury or made false statements to Congress.

* **The Charge:** On February 10, 2009, federal prosecutors filed criminal charges against Tejada in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. He was charged with a federal misdemeanor count of **making misrepresentations to Congress**.
* **The Plea:** On February 11, 2009, Tejada officially entered a guilty plea. In his plea agreement, Tejada admitted that he had lied to congressional staffers when he stated he had no knowledge of players purchasing or using PEDs. He admitted to buying HGH from Piatt, though his defense maintained that he threw the drugs away without ever using them.

### **4. Sentencing and Penalties**
On March 26, 2009, U.S. Magistrate Judge Alan Kay sentenced Tejada. 

Prosecutors acknowledged that Tejada had cooperated with investigators once charged and did not push for prison time. Judge Kay handed down the following sentence:
* **One year of probation**
* **100 hours of community service**
* **A $5,000 fine**

Tejada issued a public apology outside the courthouse, stating he was deeply sorry for making a mistake and taking the matter lightly during his initial 2005 interview.

---

### **5. Subsequent Fall-Out**
The court case severely impacted Tejada’s legacy, which previously included six All-Star selections and the 2002 American League MVP award. 

While Tejada avoided prison time, his PED-related issues did not end in federal court. In August 2013, while playing for the Kansas City Royals, MLB suspended Tejada for **105 games** after he tested positive for Adderall without an active Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE). It was one of the longest non-lifetime suspensions in MLB history at the time, effectively ending his Major League career.

---

**Summary Impact:** 
The Miguel Tejada prosecution served as a critical precedent during the federal government's crackdown on sports dishonesty, sending a clear message that lying to congressional investigators regarding drug use carried formal criminal consequences, regardless of an athlete's status.

Piatt provided checks signed by Tejada as evidence of the transactions. The Mitchell Report noted that while there was clear evidence Tejada purchased the substances, it was unclear if he had actually used them.

Following the release of the Mitchell Report, committee leaders requested that the Department of Justice investigate whether Tejada had committed perjury during his 2005 interview.

### Latest Blow to Baseball’s "Steroid Era"

Tejada, a six-time All-Star who won the American League MVP award in 2002 with the Athletics, currently plays shortstop for the Houston Astros. Neither Tejada's legal team nor representatives for the Astros immediately returned requests for comment Tuesday. 

Major League Baseball issued a brief statement acknowledging the charges, stating the league "continues to cooperate fully with federal authorities in all matters relating to performance-enhancing substances."

Tejada joins a growing list of high-profile athletes ensnared in legal trouble related to congressional and federal investigations into the "steroid era." Home run king Barry Bonds and legendary pitcher Roger Clemens have both faced federal charges related to alleged false statements regarding PED use.

*CNN's Legal and Sports Units contributed to this report.*
